content:
Few pieces of alleged Bigfoot evidence have generated as much discussion as the Freeman footage, filmed by former U.S. Forest Service patrolman and Bigfoot researcher Paul Freeman in the Blue Mountains of the Pacific Northwest.

The grainy footage appears to show a large, human-like, hair covered figure moving through the forest and depending on how the later portion is interpreted, possibly more than one Sasquatch.

Who Was Paul Freeman?

Paul Freeman (1943–2003) was a longtime Bigfoot investigator who became known for documenting alleged Sasquatch tracks as well as reporting personal encounters. His background as a Forest Service patrolman gave him considerable experience in the wilderness, and he spent years investigating reports and physical traces that he believed were connected to Sasquatch.

The 1994 Blue Mountains Encounter

The footage generally known as the Freeman footage was reportedly recorded in the Blue Mountains of northeastern Oregon. Sources differ over the exact date, with some accounts giving 1994 and others arguing for 1992. The 1994 date is the one most commonly associated with the footage.

According to accounts of the encounter, Freeman was following a trail of what he believed were fresh Sasquatch footprints. He filmed the tracks and followed them through the forest. At some point, his camera captured a large, dark, apparently bipedal figure moving across an opening in the trees.

The Mysterious “Baby Lift”

Perhaps the most intriguing part of the Freeman footage comes later.

When the footage was examined and enhanced, some researchers argued that another Sasquatch or possibly a juvenile can be seen in the distance. In the commonly discussed interpretation, an adult figure appears to reach down and lift a much smaller figure. This has become known as the “baby lift.”

In August of 2025 Todd Hale and I make a trip to the site of the famous Paul Freeman footage of a Sasquatch 33 years later. While there I captured some footage of the local wildlife as well as some suspicious audio indicating the area is still viable for Sasquatch research.
